title: Certificates: who a server is
summary: What a certificate says, the chain up to a root you trust, the names it covers, and why it ends.

scheme: └── issuer        Lab CA, who signed all this
text: A certificate is a public key with a promise attached: this key belongs to these names, until this date. A CA (certificate authority) checked it and signed the promise.
- Its private key stays on the server: it proves the server is the one the certificate talks about.
- Anyone can copy a certificate. Without its private key, it's useless.
Nobody knows every server. Your system keeps a short list of root CAs it trusts: the trust store.
- Roots sign intermediates, and intermediates sign the servers' certificates.
- The server sends its own certificate and the intermediates. The client follows the signatures up to a root it already has.
- An intermediate missing, and the chain breaks, even if each certificate is fine. A browser may fetch the missing one by itself, but curl and openssl don't: "works in my browser" proves nothing.
The client checks that the name you asked for is in the certificate's SAN (Subject Alternative Name).
- The CN in the subject is an old place for a name: browsers don't read it, only the SAN.
- shop.example and www.shop.example are two names. A certificate covers only the ones it lists.
- *.shop.example covers one level: www.shop.example yes, shop.example no.
A certificate works between two dates. After the second one, every client refuses it: the site is down for everyone at once.
- Public certificates live shorter and shorter (CA/Browser Forum rules): renewing by hand stops working.
- So renewing is a program's job (certbot and its timer), and so is checking: exit status 1 = it ends within 30 days.
